newsitem.title: CHINA: China's state firms a focus of bank conference.
newsitem.headline: China's state firms a focus of bank conference.

text.p: China began a national banking policy conference on Monday where lending to the ailing state sector was expected to be a key issue, the official Xinhua news agency said.

Thousands of officials from the central bank and commercial banks around the country were gathering in Beijing to discuss policy issues for the new year. Major commercial banks would also hold their own internal policy meetings during the week.

A major topic at the national conference would be the banks' relations with state-owned companies, most of them undergoing restructuring or struggling to survive as China shifts its once centrally planned economy to free market principles, Xinhua said in an overnight report.
Bank officials would discuss how to continue their drive to lend funds on commercial terms but still help struggling state companies, the news agency said.
"Over the past few years, local banks have tried hard to help state firms, but with the fear that the banks themselves may be saddled with accumulated bad loans," it said.
China has been trying to reform its ailing state companies, which are no longer protected by central planning, and make them better able to compete in the sink-or-swim marketplace.

About 75 percent of its more than 100,000 state firms lost money last year and total losses in the government sector soared to 69 billion yuan ($8.3 billion) between January and October, a year-on-year rise of 45 percent.
China has also been trying to make its banking sector extend loans on a commercial basis and move away from past practices of lending based on policy decisions.
Such practices discouraged borrowers from repaying loans and made banks little more than vehicles for pumping funds into state firms regardless of their prospects for making a profit.
China has created separate policy banks to make loans it sees as needed by key state sectors but only priority areas are likely to be eligible and this has many state firms worried.
Xinhua said bankruptcies would also be discussed.

Dai Xianglong, governor of the People's Bank of China, the central bank, warned last week that banks would fight illegal bankruptcies and that China's bankruptcy law had to protect both banks and failing enterprises.
Enterprises would need the approval of their main creditors before they were allowed to declare bankruptcy, he said.
The meeting would also turn its attention to intensified competition in the domestic market from foreign banks.

Four foreign banks have been cleared so far to conduct business in local currency in Shanghai and more banks are expected to gain approval this year. Previously, foreign banks could only accept deposits and make loans in foreign currency.
